newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani dealers favour cotton commission houses.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani dealers favour cotton commission houses.

text.p: Pakistani dealers have suggested the setting up of cotton commission houses to check cotton quality, keep prices range-bound, help exports and facilitate availability, traders and analysts said on Wednesday.
"The cotton commission houses would play a key role in the cotton business," Nadershaw D. Kabraji, chairman of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) told Reuters in an interview.
Such houses, with storage capacity of about a half million 375-lb bales, should be located at the industrial port city of Karachi, Kabraji said. "These would basically help the export of cotton."

Broker Nasim Usman said the idea of setting up such houses was not new as they existed before the creation of the state-run Cotton Export Corporation (CEC) in the early 1970s, when cotton exports were nationalised.
"The houses would help in storing ginners stocks, buying of cotton by textile mills and exporters on the basis of quality and keep prices within limits," Usman said.
He said the need for reviving these houses was felt after some 1.4 million bales of unsold cotton piled up at ginneries when mills failed to pick up stocks due to liquidity problems.
"The ginners are now appealing to the government to ask the CEC to buy the unsold stocks," he said.
Usman said mills have already utilised bank credit limits, available to them at lower interest rates. "The mills cannot get fresh credit limits unless they repay the previous loan."
He said the 24 percent interest rate being charged by banks on regular loans was discouraging mills from holding stocks for a longer period. "Many mills were operating on hand-to-mouth basis."

Usman said banks could be asked to extend rotating credit to the commission houses to enable them to buy substantial quantities of cotton from ginners and store them for mills and exports. "The houses could also store cotton as buffer stocks."
Kabraji said ginners would benefit from these houses as they would get 75 percent of the price of the cotton on arrival at these houses and the remainder after the full sale.
"The houses would take pressure off ginners as it will open one more avenue of sales," Kabraji said.

Total cotton crop production is likely to reach 9.35 million bales and from ginneries 8.8 million during the current 1996/97 year (July-June), down from a target of 10 million and compared with 9.94 million production in 1995/96, said an official of the Ministry of Food and Agriculture.
An official of the KCA said the government had fixed a target of 10 million bales for 1997/98.

Broker Khushi Ram said it was too early to predict the size of the 1997/98 crop, but agreed that it would be higher than 1996/97 output as farmers were paying more attention to cotton crop than sugarcane due to its higher prices in domestic markets.
Fasihuddin, secretary of the KCA, said exporters had shipped 31,647 bales between September 1 and March 24, compared with 1.594 million in the same time a year-ago.
